From ₹265 cr to ₹1,531 cr. That is how much bank borrowing Crisil now rates for Archean Chemical, and it explains why the agency cut the company's long-term rating to A-/Stable from A/Negative.

The bromine and salt maker is building a silicon carbide semiconductor plant through a step-down subsidiary, SiCSem. Crisil says the project cost has risen to about ₹2,500 cr from about ₹2,100 cr, mainly due to the weaker rupee and higher procurement costs. Roughly ₹900-1,000 cr of the remaining spend is to come from term loans, most of the rest from government incentives.

Crisil expects debt to climb from ₹466 cr in March 2026 to ₹1,100-1,200 cr a year later. Net debt could reach 3.5-3.8 times yearly operating profit (EBITDA), against 1.53 times in FY26, and the chip plant is not expected to bring in cash before FY29.

The old business is not carrying it as easily either. Crisil notes bromine volumes fell about 25% in FY26 and the Q1 operating margin slipped to 20.6% from 26.7%.

The rating agency's own warning is plain: delays, further cost overruns or a slow ramp-up would add pressure, while an equity raise or quick release of grants would ease it.

The contract was a ₹413 crore engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) package for 400 MWh of battery storage at NTPC's Mouda Super Thermal Power Station. NTPC awarded it to G R Infraprojects (GRIL) in March 2026. Six months in, GRIL issued a termination notice, citing force majeure and war risk linked to the West Asia conflict. NTPC says critical activities were delayed and treats the termination as a default by the contractor. GRIL has disputed the invocation, and the matter has gone to dispute resolution.

NTPC invoked ₹90.86 crore of security on 17 September, two days after GRIL's termination notice. This was a ₹49.53 crore mobilisation advance bank guarantee and ₹41.34 crore in Insurance Surety Bonds for performance security. Both were paid on the same day.

For insurers that issue Insurance Surety Bonds in India, three points stand out.

The insurer paid on the same day as the bank. A Maharatna company invoked an Insurance Surety Bond alongside a bank guarantee, and NTPC received both amounts on 17 September. Procurement teams now have a recorded case of an Insurance Surety Bond paying out on invocation alongside a bank guarantee.

The contractor was financially strong. GRIL is rated Crisil AA. Crisil reports that GRIL sought contractual relief because of market conditions after the West Asia conflict, and NTPC did not grant it. Insurers who price mainly on a contractor's financials would have seen a comfortable risk here. Force majeure clauses, price variation terms and tenor need the same scrutiny as the contractor's books.

The contractor repaid both issuers. Crisil reports that GRIL had kept funds with the bank and the insurer and honoured the full ₹90.86 crore on the same day. CARE Ratings reports that GRIL funded the amounts payable to both. Under a bank guarantee and an Insurance Surety Bond alike, the issuer pays the beneficiary and the contractor repays the issuer. Neither report says what margin, if any, the insurer held when it issued the bonds. 
That margin decides how much working capital a contractor frees by choosing an Insurance Surety Bond.

More storage contracts are coming. NTPC Green Energy (NGEL) invited bids in September for a 3.3 GWh storage project at Khavda, due on 27 October. NTPC told analysts after its Q4 FY26 results that about 5 GWh of storage is being built at its thermal stations, and Mouda was one of those projects. Insurers will be asked to issue Insurance Surety Bonds for performance security on these contracts.

#RelianceJio IPO: The comparison needs a stronger foundation.

Your concern about valuation deserves discussion. But comparing Jio with AT&T and Verizon primarily through current revenue and market capitalisation produces an incomplete investment argument.

1. Mature American telecom companies cannot automatically set Jio’s valuation ceiling.

AT&T and Verizon are useful reference points. Their multiples still require adjustments for growth, debt, spectrum obligations, capital expenditure, competitive intensity and market opportunity.

Comparing equity market capitalisations while overlooking those differences is financially inadequate. Compare enterprise values, sustainable free cash flows and returns on incremental capital.

Jio does not need to match AT&T’s revenue before deserving a comparable equity valuation. A smaller business can command greater value if its future cash generation justifies it.

2. More than 500 million customers are an extraordinary starting position.

Jio reported 533.3 million customers in June 2026, including 503.6 million mobile broadband customers. That gives it enormous distribution, customer relationships and a base across which to spread technology investment. India still offers opportunities in connectivity upgrades, home broadband and enterprise digitisation. 

The investment question is how much additional value Jio can earn from that base.

Illustratively, an additional ₹10 monthly revenue across 500 million customers means ₹6,000 crore in annual revenue, before costs, taxes and customer changes.

American ARPU is unnecessary for that arithmetic to become meaningful.

3. The claim that ARPU cannot rise is contradicted by Jio’s own experience.

CRISIL reports that Jio’s monthly ARPU increased from ₹131 in FY2020 to ₹214 in FY2026, approximately 8.5% CAGR, reaching ₹215.6 in Q1 FY2027. Historical affordability does not establish a permanent ceiling on monetisation.

Growth can also come through better service bundles and customer upgrades. Reliance already reports monetisation across content, cloud, IoT and managed services. 

4. Owning the technology stack changes the opportunity.

Jio markets its own portfolio spanning radio, core, network automation and operational software to other telecom operators. This creates a credible route to supplying low-cost, high-quality services globally, including under an overseas operator’s own brand through white-label arrangements.

The potential economics matter: Jio could earn technology and managed-service revenue overseas without financing an entire consumer network in every country.

Its subsidiary Radisys already offers a white-label communications platform.

5. Low prices can reveal engineering strength.

The bullish argument is that Indian engineering, proprietary software, automation and enormous scale can create a structural cost advantage.

The valuable capability is delivering more utility at a sustainably lower cost.

6. Even the US opportunity should remain open.

Could Jio eventually supply technology to American operators, including in the 6G era? Potentially. Its disclosed technology development includes 6G. Treat it as additional upside with an uncertain probability. 

7. Being among India’s five largest companies places no mathematical ceiling on returns.

Returns depend on earnings growth, cash generation, reinvestment and the entry valuation. Market-cap rank alone cannot answer the question.

A small float can distort early pricing. Currency depreciation and future investment requirements deserve scrutiny. Those are valid valuation inputs.

But the central question remains:

What price fairly values Jio’s Indian cash flows, its cost advantage and its opportunity to export technology?

A bullish thesis must survive that calculation. A bearish thesis must address it too.

Productive ambition deserves rigorous valuation. Yesterday’s industry hierarchy cannot substitute for that work.

The cost of Winning ft. INSTAHELP  vs BLINKIT

There is a part of the "winner-take-all" story in quick commerce that I think is worth remembering as we look at Urban Company’s InstaHelp.

Blinkit is often used as proof that quick commerce eventually works. And it does show that a player can go through years of heavy investment and losses and eventually build a profitable business at scale.

But there is another side to that story.

In Q4 FY26, Zepto reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹1,248 Cr and Swiggy Instamart reported a loss of ₹858 Cr, while Blinkit reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹37 Cr.

The point isn't that Zepto or Instamart will fail. It is that a winner-take-most market can require enormous investment from multiple players before the eventual economics become clear.

And this is exactly what makes Urban Company's InstaHelp interesting.

Urban Company has explicitly said that InstaHelp is its most significant long-term investment. In Q4 FY26, it reported a ₹119 Cr adjusted EBITDA loss in the business and said losses would remain elevated as it invested to cement leadership.

By Q1 FY27, the loss had increased to ₹132 Cr, even as orders grew 43% QoQ to 3.82 million and loss per order improved from ₹447 to ₹346.

That is the interesting tension.

If this really is a winner-take-all or winner-take-most market, then being early and building density could matter enormously.

But winning also means being willing to fund the network before the economics fully show up.

Urban Company's bet is essentially that density creates a flywheel: more demand → better partner utilisation → better earnings → better supply retention → faster fulfilment → more demand.

If that flywheel works, today's losses could be investments in future market structure.

If it doesn't, the same losses simply become the cost of competing in an attractive category.

That's why I wouldn't look at InstaHelp's ₹132 Cr quarterly loss in isolation.

I'd watch whether each additional rupee of investment is buying greater density, utilisation and repeat behaviour -and whether those improvements eventually translate into structurally better unit economics OR  eventual market leadership position.

That's the real test of the winner-take-all thesis.
Not whether Urban Company can grow fast. Whether it can turn the cost of winning into an economic moat.

Religion and Science
Religion and Science are diametrically opposed to each other. They are poles apart, and it is nonsense to say that they compliment each other.

1. Religion says that there is a supernatural entity called God, which is immortal, permanent, all powerful, merciful, all good, etc

Science does not believe in supernatural entities. It does not believe anything in the Universe is permanent. Everything is changing and in flux, in accordance with some laws, which can be discovered by scientific research.

Science holds that there are no supernatural entities like God, angels, fairies, demons,witches or soul ( and therefore there is no such thing as transmigration of the soul, or resurrection on Judgment Day ), and that nothing is permanent, everything is changing, and in a state of flux, in accordance with certain laws which can be discovered by scientific research.

Science holds that the only reality is matter, which is in motion according to certain laws.
Some people ask : who created matter ? The answer is : there is no creator of matter. Matter came from matter, though the form keeps changing.

2. With every step science advances, religion recedes. Thus, people at one time thought that small pox is due to the anger of a goddess ( mata ), but now we know it is because of a virus, and can be prevented by innoculation. People at one time thought that rains are caused by a rain god, Indra, and so if there is drought we have to propitiate that god in some way ( many people in India still believe that ). Today we know that rains are caused by the build up of low pressure areas over a heated land. People at one time believed that Adam and Eve were created by God. Later Darwin proved that men evolved from the apes.

3. Religion relies on faith and divine revelation.
Science relies on observation, experiment and reason.

4. Religion claims to say the final word, and cannot be changed. Thus, the Vedas, the Quran, the Bible, etc cannot be changed.
In science there is no final word, and scientific theories can, and have been, regularly tested and changed.

For example, Newton said in 1666 that light travelled as particles ( the corpuscular theory ). But in
1678 the Dutch scientist Huygens' propunded his Fresnel principle that light travelled as waves. Much later Max Planck propounded his Quantum theory which said that light travelled as discrete particles. Still later, Quantum mechanics, as propounded by De Broglie, and as developed by Heisenberg, Schrodinger, etc, said that particles can be conceived of as waves ( and vice versa )

5. Religion says that the Universe was created at a particular time by God, with all living beings. But Darwin proved by his theory of evolution, that creatures have evolved.

6. Religion says that there has to be a Creator of the Universe, which is God.

Science says that there is no such Creator. The only reality in the Universe is matter ( or rather matter-energy, since matter and energy are two forms of the same substance, as Einstein proved ), and matter is in motion, in accordance with certain laws, which can be discovered by scientific research. If it is asked where did matter come from, the answer is matter came from matter.

If it is said that every thing must have a creator, then that creator too must have a creator. i.e. a super creator, and that super creator too must have a creator, i.e. a super super creator, and so on. This is known as the fallacy of the infinite regress.

7. Religion says that God is all powerful, merciful and all good. If that is so, then why do millions of children in the world suffer from hunger, cold, etc ? Why does God, who is said to be merciful, not have mercy on them and give them food, clothes, shelter, etc ?

Why is there so much poverty, unemployment, malnourishment, sickness etc in the world ? If God is
powerful and merciful, why does he not abolish these and give everyone a decent life ?
It is true that some scientists believed in God. But that only proves that scientific and unscientific ideas can co-exist in the same head, and it will take a long time, probably several generations, before unscientific ideas are altogether eliminated

All religions are superstitions and false. The truth lies in science, which is constantly developing.
If India is to progress, we must go over from religion to science
